title: What To Do When Students Ignore Your Instructions uctions/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses moments when students blatantly disregard clear, familiar instructions, arguing that lectures, threats, and warnings settle things temporarily but fail to prevent recurrence. He proposes a structured response: wait silently for students to sense the gravity of the situation, test them with a simple direction, cancel upcoming plans to make time for a full reteach, mimic the exact misbehavior without naming names, model the correct way seriously (given safety implications), have students redo the activity under the same conditions, move on immediately once they succeed, and return to the original context (like the library) as soon as possible. He frames this as turning a frustrating moment into a memorable teaching opportunity rather than a battle of wills.
points: Blatant disregard for known instructions calls for an eight-step corrective sequence rather than lectures or warnings, which don't prevent recurrence.
The sequence begins with silent waiting, followed by testing compliance with a simple direction before deciding whether a full reteach is needed.
Mimicking student misbehavior without naming names, followed by a serious (not humorous) model of correct behavior, is a core part of the reteach.
Students should redo the activity under conditions matching the original misbehavior, then the teacher should move on immediately without dwelling on it.
Returning to the same context (e.g., the library) as soon as possible lets students fully leave the incident behind them.
quotes: The truth is, if you look real close, if you sneak up quietly, part the tall grass, and examine the situation with a bit of shrewdness, you’ll see an opportunity just waiting to be had… An opportunity to teach your students a lesson they’ll not soon forget.

Without mentioning names, mimic for your students the behaviors you witnessed. Be as exacting as possible. With rare exception, whatever you act out for your students in detail, they’ll go to great pains not to do again.
Disregarding your direct instructions is a serious offense—with safety implications. As such, affect a serious tone as you model the right way to do things.
Too many teachers undermine these opportunities by belaboring the point, harping on it until the students are resentful and ready for revolt.
Effective classroom management is about action. It’s about doing something in response to misbehavior. It’s about communicating what you want then holding students accountable for doing it.
